hook: The entire species lives on one shelf, eleven feet by sixteen.

story.text: Every wild Devils Hole pupfish lives in one desert cavern, a pool over five hundred feet deep with no mapped bottom.
They feed and spawn almost entirely on one sunlit shelf near the surface, eleven feet by sixteen, under a foot deep.
The water stays near 92°F and low in oxygen; the fish are an inch long, with no pelvic fins.
Males turn shimmering blue, females stay yellow-brown, and most live about a year.
When ranch wells drew the pool down, the Supreme Court ruled in 1976 that reserving Devils Hole in 1952 had reserved the water to keep its shelf wet.
Twice a year since 1972, three agencies count every fish, from the surface and on scuba below a hundred feet.
The spring count fell to 35 fish in 2013, then climbed to 191 by April 2024, the most in 25 years.
Then distant earthquakes in December 2024 and February 2025 sent six-foot waves through the pool, stripping the shelf of algae and eggs; the next count found 38.
For the first time, biologists released 19 fish reared from shelf-gathered eggs in a 100,000-gallon replica cavern at Ash Meadows; by spring 2026 the count was 77.
To witness the Devils Hole pupfish is to keep watch over the smallest home of any vertebrate: one shelf, one pool, one aquifer.

reproduction.text: Spawning goes on at a low level all year and peaks with the longest days; eggs are laid on the shelf, and each month some are lifted from recovery mats and carried to the refuge tank to hatch.

insight.text: The whole species feeds and breeds on about 215 square feet of limestone — roughly the floor of a one-car garage — the smallest range of any vertebrate on the planet.
